newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica privatisation proceeding speedily - Transnet.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica privatisation proceeding speedily - Transnet.

text.p: The privatisation of South African state assets was proceeding more quickly than was generally believed, said Saki Macozoma, incoming managing director of Transnet, the country's transportation parastatal.
"The restructuring of state assets is proceeding quicker than most people believe," Macozoma told journalists at the presentation of Transnet's annual results on Wednesday.
Government recently announced that it had earmarked transport as the second sector to be assessed for privatisation after telecommunications.
Macozoma declined to comment further on the process.
"The matter is being discussed in the National Framework Agreement (NFA) -- an agreement between government and labour unions -- and no one is allowed to talk outside that," Macozoma said.
In its 1995/96 annual report released on Wednesday, Transnet said it had put forward to the NFA some tentative views on its own restructuring.

Government privatisation adviser Kennedy Memani last month said officials were in the process of identifying separate entities within the tranportation sector, ranging from road transportation to South African Airways (SAA), and drafting a range of options for each.
Transnet subsidiaries include SAA, Autonet (road transport), Petronet (oil pipeline), Spoornet (railways), PX (container and parcel delivery) and Portnet (ports).

Macozoma said the restructuring of Transnet could be hurt by the continued deficit on Transnet's pension fund which at March 31 stood at 3.2 billion rand compared to 4.2 billion a year ago. Steps had been taken to address the problem.
"We have requested the Minister of Finance to see how the pension question can be resolved in such a way that it does not detract from the value of our assets," Macozoma said.
He said the ministry, which was investigating new retirement dispensations including a provident fund, would report back in mid-November with a decision from the minister expected a month later.
The deficit dates back to the formation of Transnet in 1991 when it inherited the South African Transport Services' pension fund with a shortfall of 17 billion rand.
Transnet director Eugene Kruger said it would take nine years for the deficit to be fully funded, although this could be shortened if investment returns beat expectations.
Transnet on Wednesday reported a 253 million rand loss in the year to March 31, compared to a 118 million profit a year ago, with the PX and Spoornet divisions the poorest performers.
